action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic and infective precipitants; here also the severity of sepsis (lactate, creatinine) [ACG_HE_2026]

action_criteria.rationale: Every hospitalised patient with cirrhosis, ascites and encephalopathy needs a diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP, here even though a urinary source is evident

action_criteria.label: Medication review: antibiotic for ciprofloxacin-resistant E. coli bacteremia with kidney injury; propranolol and diuretics in sepsis; sedatives
action_criteria.rationale: A recent fluoroquinolone course, kidney injury and sepsis change the antibiotic choice and the safety of her beta-blocker and diuretics [EASL_decomp_2018]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.
Do not treat with a fluoroquinolone: the E. coli is ciprofloxacin-resistant after a recent course.
required_recommendations: Sepsis care: cultures then IV antibiotic within one hour, volume with albumin, monitor lactate, urine output and creatinine, ICU review if hypotension persists (EASL 2018).

Empirical IV antibiotic for E. coli urosepsis (ceftriaxone 2 g daily, or piperacillin-tazobactam if a resistant organism is suspected after the recent ciprofloxacin course), then narrowed to the susceptibilities (ceftriaxone-susceptible, ciprofloxacin-resistant) for 7-14 days according to response; no fluoroquinolone and no aminoglycoside.
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Kidney injury (creatinine 1.6 mg/dL) with sodium 126 mEq/L: stop spironolactone, furosemide and propranolol, give IV albumin 1 g/kg (up to 100 g) per day for two days, replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more, raise the sodium by no more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours, and monitor creatinine and urine output (EASL 2018).

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury. Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily.
Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose (heavy alcohol use).

Refer for liver transplant assessment once the sepsis is controlled: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 35 (EASL 2018); offer treatment for alcohol use disorder, since continued drinking precludes listing.
Address recurrent UTI etiology in outpatient follow-up.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 35), precipitated by E. coli urosepsis with bacteremia (recurrent UTI after a recent ciprofloxacin course); ascites requires SBP exclusion.

differential.key_features: Ascites in an infected cirrhotic makes a tap mandatory regardless of the urinary source; the ascitic PMN of 186 cells/mm3 (below 250) with a sterile culture excludes SBP.

differential.diagnosis: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy as the sole cause
differential.key_features: E. coli bacteremia with lactate 3.4 mmol/L, BP 104/64 and HR 116 contributes to the encephalopathy; asterixis, jaundice and advanced liver failure point to HE precipitated by the sepsis, and the two coexist.

differential.diagnosis: Acute alcohol intake (daughter reports drinking 2 weeks ago)
differential.key_features: Contributing precipitant via dehydration and ammonia load; not the primary current driver.
Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL in sepsis is kidney injury; HRS-AKI cannot be diagnosed until the infection is treated and volume is restored with albumin.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Any infection in cirrhosis (UTI, pneumonia, cellulitis, SBP, bacteremia) can precipitate HE through cytokine-mediated hepatic dysfunction and increased ammonia production.
Child-Pugh C (15: bilirubin 12.4 3, albumin 2.0 3, INR 2.8 3, large ascites 3, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 35 (creatinine 1.6, bilirubin 12.4, INR 2.8, sodium 126)

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
A urinary isolate after a recent fluoroquinolone course is likely to be fluoroquinolone-resistant: empirical therapy must not rely on ciprofloxacin.
